message.content:
Below is a concise, up‑to‑date overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas (as of 2026). It’s meant as a quick reference; for specific situations you may want to consult a local attorney or the Texas Attorney General’s Office. | Area | What You’re Generally Entitled To | Practical Tips | |------|-----------------------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge a *maximum* of **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., damage beyond normal wear). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Texas law requires landlords to repair major defects that affect health or safety. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep a copy.
• If repairs aren’t made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent or pursue a “repair‑and‑deduct” remedy (see below). | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a **material defect** that makes the unit uninhabitable, you may pay for the repair yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, **up to the amount of the rent**. | • Keep receipts and document the issue.
• Notify the landlord in writing before making the repair. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlords can raise rent only at the end of a **fixed‑term lease** or at the start of a new lease.
• No statutory cap on increases, but you can negotiate or refuse to renew. | • Review the lease for any “rent‑increase” clauses. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month** tenants can terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• Fixed‑term leases must be honored unless both parties agree to terminate or the landlord breaches. | • Provide written notice (email or letter) and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must give **30 days’ written notice** for non‑payment of rent.
• For other reasons (lease violation, no‑fault eviction), the landlord must follow the proper notice period (usually 30 days for non‑payment, 30–60 days for other violations).
• Texas courts require a **formal eviction lawsuit** if the tenant does not vacate after notice. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you believe the eviction is unlawful, file a **motion to dismiss** or seek a **temporary restraining order**. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Attorney General or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) if you suspect discrimination. | | **Fair Housing** | • Texas law protects against discrimination in housing. | • Keep records of any discriminatory actions. | | **Utilities & Services** | • Landlord must provide essential services (water, heat, electricity) unless otherwise specified in the lease. | • Verify which utilities you are responsible for. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord’s consent. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Remedies** | • **Small claims court** (up to $20,000) for disputes over deposits, damages, or unpaid rent.
• **Civil action** for breach of lease or unlawful eviction.
• **Mediation** is often encouraged before litigation. | • Keep all documentation (lease, receipts, correspondence). | ### Quick Checklist Before Moving In 1. **Read the Lease Thoroughly** – Pay special attention to: - Security deposit limits - Maintenance responsibilities - Notice periods for termination or entry - Pet policies - Rent increase clauses 2. **Document the Unit** – Take dated photos or videos of all rooms, fixtures, and any existing damage. Sign a move‑in inspection form with the landlord. 3. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections (rent control, eviction moratoria, etc.). 4. **Keep Copies of All Communication** – Emails, texts, letters, and notes from phone calls. 5. **Know the Eviction Timeline** – If you receive a notice, act quickly. Texas law gives landlords a limited window to file an eviction suit after notice. ### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Housing** | Tenant rights guide, complaint filing instructions. | | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Information on fair housing, landlord‑tenant laws. | | **Texas Small Claims Court** | How to file a claim for deposit disputes or damages. | | **Local Legal Aid Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance (e.g., Texas Legal Services Center). | | **HUD’s Fair Housing Hotline** | 1‑800‑669‑6767 (for discrimination complaints). | --- #### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, a clear lease, timely notice for any changes, and protection against unlawful eviction or discrimination. Keep detailed records, communicate in writing, and know the timelines for notices and legal actions. If you encounter a problem, you can often resolve it through written communication, mediation, or, if necessary, small‑claims court. For complex disputes, consider consulting a tenant‑rights attorney.
